blocks.text: I can measure extensions of a spring for a good range of stretching forces.
You will plan an experiment where weights pull on a spring, and learn how to measure the results accurately.

items.title: Measuring the extension of a spring

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: The extension of a spring is the change in length.
Masses will have a gravitational force that pulls them downwards.
Hanging masses (weights) can be used to put a known force onto a spring.
A mass hanger can be attached to a spring; adding masses to it causes the spring to stretch in a controlled way.

blocks.text: Pull on the end of a spring and the coils move further apart. The spring gets longer. We say it has {extended}.
The {extension} is the increase in length. The larger the stretching force, the greater the extension.

blocks.label: Watch out!
blocks.text: The length of the spring is not the extension. The extension is only how much LONGER the spring has become.

blocks.q: A spring is 9.0 cm long with no force on it. With a force on it, it is 15.5 cm long. What is its extension?

blocks.text: If you just pull a spring by hand, the force is uncontrolled and you cannot measure it. To get a controlled force we hang masses from a **mass hanger** on the end of the spring.
The mass hanger and each 100 g mass pull down on the spring with an extra force of {1 N} each.

blocks.q: Each 100 g mass and the hanger pull down with 1 N each.

items.q: What is the total downward force from a hanger and 2 masses?
What is the total downward force from a hanger and 5 masses?

blocks.text: Adding a mass pulls down harder, so the spring stretches more.
You will test whether there is a pattern in the relationship between the force on a spring and its extension.

items.title: Vertical ruler
items.sub: zero level with the bottom of the spring

blocks.text: Line up the {zero on the ruler} exactly with the {bottom of the spring} before you add any masses.

items.q: A pupil’s ruler is tilted to one side. What is the problem?
options: The ruler should be vertical or the readings will be wrong

items.q: Which piece of equipment makes it easier to keep the measuring line level with the bottom of the spring, giving more accurate readings?

blocks.text: A set square is easier to keep level (horizontal) than a second ruler, so it helps you read the scale more accurately.
With the ruler’s zero at the bottom of the unloaded spring, you can read the extension straight off the ruler: the reading at the bottom of the stretched spring IS the extension.

**Example.** A 1 N force pulls the bottom of the spring down to the 3.0 cm mark. The extension is 3.0 cm. Add another 100 g mass (2 N) and the spring reaches the 6.0 cm mark. The extension is now 6.0 cm.

blocks.q: With zero lined up, the bottom of a loaded spring is at the 8.5 cm mark. What is the extension?
blocks.why: Zero was lined up with the bottom of the unloaded spring, so the reading is the extension.

blocks.text: You add masses one at a time up to 6 N in total, then take them off one at a time. You do not want to overextend the spring.

blocks.q: Which stage does each step belong to?

items.text: Line up zero on the ruler with the bottom of the spring
Hang the spring from a clamp stand
Put on one more 100 g mass and measure the extension
Take off one mass and measure the extension again

blocks.text: Record two sets of extensions in a table: one as you add the masses (loading) and one as you remove them (unloading).

items: Extension when loading (cm) in the second column
Extension when unloading (cm) in the third column

blocks.text: Your values will be different from someone else’s, but the pattern should be the same: the greater the force, the bigger the extension.
Two sets of data can show whether the measurements were accurate.
If the loading and unloading results match closely, with only small differences, the measurements are {accurate}. If they are very different, some readings may be inaccurate.

blocks.q: Which pupil’s results were measured most accurately for the same force?
blocks.why: The two readings are closest together (only 0.1 cm apart), so the measurements match closely.

blocks.text: A **scientific diagram** shows how equipment is set up and used. It can also show how measurements should be made.

blocks.q: Match each item in a diagram to what it does.

pairs.b: Holds the masses on the end of the spring
Helps you read the scale level with the bottom of the spring

items.q: What does the extension of a spring tell you?
options: How long it is in total
How much its length has changed

items.q: You add more masses to the hanger. What happens to the extension?
A spring is 14.0 cm long unloaded and 17.5 cm long with a force. What is the extension?

items: A spring extends (gets longer) when a force pulls on it. Extension is the increase in length.
The greater the force, the bigger the extension.
A mass hanger with 100 g masses gives controlled forces: 1 N for the hanger and 1 N for each mass.
Line up zero on the ruler with the bottom of the spring. A set square helps accuracy.
Measure while loading and unloading. If both sets match closely, the measurements are accurate.

flashcards.front: What happens to a spring when a force pulls on it?
flashcards.back: It extends (gets longer): the coils move further apart.

flashcards.front: What is the extension of a spring?
A spring is 12 cm long unloaded and 16 cm long when stretched. What is the extension?
What is a mass hanger used for?
flashcards.back: It attaches to a spring, and masses are added to it to make the spring stretch in a controlled way.

flashcards.front: What force do the mass hanger and each 100 g mass pull down with?
flashcards.back: 1 N each (a hanger and two masses give 3 N).

flashcards.front: What are hanging masses used for?
flashcards.back: To put a known force onto a spring.

flashcards.front: How do you set up the ruler before measuring extensions?
flashcards.back: Vertical, with its zero exactly level with the bottom of the spring.

flashcards.front: Why use a set square when measuring an extension?
flashcards.back: It is easier to keep level, so the readings are more accurate.

flashcards.front: Why measure the extension as masses are taken off, as well as when they are added?
flashcards.back: If the loading and unloading measurements match closely, the measurements are accurate.

flashcards.front: What pattern do you expect between force and extension for a spring?
flashcards.back: The greater the force, the bigger the extension.

flashcards.front: What does a scientific diagram show?
flashcards.back: How equipment is set up and used, and how measurements should be made.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Stretching springs
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question in a word, a number or a short phrase. Give units where they are asked for.

questions.prompt: What word means the change in length of a spring when a force acts on it?
questions.explanation: The extension of a spring is its change in length.

questions.prompt: A spring is 9.0 cm long unloaded. With masses on it, it is 15.5 cm long. What is its extension? Give your answer in cm.
The mass hanger and each 100 g mass pull down with 1 N. What total force is produced by a mass hanger with 2 masses on it? Give your answer in newtons.
What is the total force from a mass hanger with 5 masses of 100 g each? Give your answer in newtons.
The ruler’s zero is lined up with the bottom of the unloaded spring. With a load, the bottom of the spring is at the 7.5 cm mark. What is the extension? Give your answer in cm.
questions.explanation: The zero is lined up with the unloaded spring, so the reading is the extension.

questions.prompt: What piece of equipment holds the masses on the end of the spring?
questions.explanation: Masses are added to a mass hanger (holder) attached to the spring.

questions.prompt: Which piece of equipment, easier to keep level than a ruler, gives more accurate readings of the extension?
questions.explanation: A set square is easier to keep level, so the readings are more accurate.

questions.prompt: Pupil A’s results for 2 N are: loading 6.0 cm and unloading 6.1 cm. Pupil B’s are: loading 6.0 cm and unloading 7.4 cm. Which pupil’s measurements match more closely, showing better accuracy? Answer A or B.
questions.explanation: A’s two readings differ by only 0.1 cm, B’s by 1.4 cm.

questions.prompt: A spring extends 3.0 cm when the force is 1 N. If the force increases, does the extension get bigger or smaller?
questions.explanation: The greater the force, the bigger the extension.
